A rule across the codes

How long do you get to keep the ball?

part of One Game, Many Codes
  • Association football
    No limit. You keep the ball until the other side takes it.
    Laws of the Game (IFAB)
  • Rugby union
    No set count. Possession is contested afresh at every tackle, ruck and maul.
    World Rugby Laws
  • Rugby league
    Six tackles, then a handover (four from 1966; six from 1972).
    RFL Laws
  • American football
    Four downs to make ten yards, or the ball changes hands.
    NFL Rules
  • Canadian football
    Three downs to make ten yards, or the ball changes hands.
    CFL Rules
  • Australian rules football
    No limit. A continuous contest for the ball.
    AFL Laws

Every code has to answer one question before anything else about it makes sense: once you have the ball, how long is it yours? The answers split the family in two — codes that never count possession, and codes that put a number on it.

Why it was introduced

Left unlimited, possession rewards holding on. In rugby league before 1966 that produced strangulation football: a side could keep the ball almost indefinitely, and did. The limited-tackle rule put a number on possession for the first time — and a number changes how a thing is spent.

On the pitch

Six tackles made possession scarce. Scarce things get spent carefully — that is why league teams kick on the last. The gridiron codes reached the same idea by a different route: a fixed count of downs to make the distance turned each possession into a sequence of planned, discrete plays, with Canadian football's three downs forcing the issue a down sooner than the American four. Where the count is absent — soccer, union, Australian rules — possession is kept until it is lost, and the game flows without a built-in reset.

In the stands

A number you can see becomes a countdown. As the last tackle nears, everyone watching knows the ball is about to change hands, and the tension climbs toward that moment — a suspense the uncounted codes never manufacture in quite the same way.

Adoption and rejection

Soccer never counted possession and shows no sign of starting. Union kept the contest open at the breakdown rather than capping it. The gridiron codes made the count spatial — yards to be gained — rather than a tally of tackles. One idea, a finite possession, arrived at independently and expressed four different ways.
